summary: Describes an optional IPv6 Router Advertisement extension for sending default router preferences and more-specific routes to hosts. It helps multi-homed hosts pick an appropriate router when routers are on different links. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4191 lets IPv6 routers advertise which default router a host should prefer and which routers can reach specific prefixes. This helps multi-homed hosts choose an appropriate next hop without changing behavior for hosts that ignore the extension.

subtitle: An IPv6 Router Advertisement extension for choosing preferred routers and advertising routes for specific prefixes.

tldr.problem: A host with several routers may choose an unsuitable router for off-link traffic, and Redirect messages cannot direct a host to a router on another link.
tldr.mechanism: Routers advertise a preference for the default route and can include Route Information Options for specific prefixes, each with its own preference and lifetime.
tldr.outcome: Hosts that implement the extension can choose a router using preferences and prefix matches; hosts that do not implement it continue to work as before. Administrators configure the advertised information.

today: RFC 4191 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2005. It defines an optional, backward-compatible extension, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Choosing Among Multiple Routers
sections.content:
IPv6 Neighbor Discovery gives a host a Default Router List and a Prefix List. The host uses the Prefix List to decide whether a destination is on-link and the Default Router List to select a router for off-link traffic. If several routers are available, selecting the wrong one can reduce performance or prevent communication.

A router can use a Redirect to recommend a different router, but a Redirect applies only on one link. It cannot direct a multi-homed host to a router on another link. RFC 4191 adds optional preference and route information to Router Advertisements. The preferences and routes require administrative configuration rather than being derived automatically from routing tables.
sections.plainLanguage: A host with several network connections may have several routers to choose from. Router Advertisements can now identify a preferred default router and advertise routes for specific destinations.

sections.title: Default Router Preference
sections.content:
The extension encodes preference as a two-bit signed value. 01 means High, 00 means Medium and is the default, and 11 means Low. The value 10 is reserved and MUST NOT be sent.

The Router Advertisement header gains a Prf field. If the Router Lifetime is zero, the sender MUST set preference to 00, and the receiver MUST ignore it. A receiver that sees the reserved value 10 treats it as 00. The RFC stresses that these three values are preferences, not routing metrics.

A Router Advertisement may also include a Route Information Option for ::/0. That option can specify a separate preference and lifetime for the default route.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can mark itself High, Medium, or Low for default-route selection. These labels express a preference, not a measure of route cost.

sections.title: Route Information Options
sections.content:
Route Information Option type 24 advertises a prefix reachable through the sending router. It includes an option length in 8-octet units, a prefix length from 0 to 128, a preference, a 32-bit Route Lifetime in seconds, and a prefix that occupies 0, 8, or 16 octets.

The option length must be 3 when the prefix length exceeds 64, and must be 2 or 3 when the prefix length is greater than zero. A lifetime of 0xffffffff means infinity. If a receiver gets the reserved preference value 10, it MUST ignore the whole option. A router MUST NOT include two options with the same prefix and prefix length in one Router Advertisement.

The RFC defines a separate option rather than extending the Prefix Information Option because a prefix typically appears in only one option, the new one is typically 16 octets rather than 32, and it may improve compatibility with some hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: A Route Information Option names a prefix, how long the route remains valid, and the preference for this router when other routers advertise the same prefix.

sections.title: Different Levels of Host Support
sections.content:
The RFC describes three conceptual host types. Type A ignores preferences and Route Information Options and follows the earlier Neighbor Discovery behavior. Type B uses default router preferences but ignores Route Information Options. Type C uses a routing table and understands both the header preference and the options.

A type C host first updates its default route from the Router Lifetime and header preference, then processes Route Information Options. A ::/0 option overrides the header's default-route preference and lifetime. A zero-lifetime route is removed; a non-zero-lifetime route is added or refreshed. When the routing table changes, the host MUST invalidate or remove affected Destination Cache entries. Type B and C hosts MAY allow local preferences to override advertised values.
sections.plainLanguage: Some hosts ignore the extension, some use only the default-router preference, and others use both preferences and prefix routes. This difference affects which advertisements guide their traffic.

sections.title: Selecting a Route and Checking Reachability
sections.content:
A type B host prefers reachable routers and then uses their preference values. A type C host looks for the matching route with the longest prefix. If routes have equal prefix length, it uses preference to choose among them. If a preferred route points to an unreachable router, the host tries the next-best route. If no route matches, a type C host SHOULD discard the packet and report Destination Unreachable/No Route To Destination.

A host with no reachability information assumes a router is reachable. When useful traffic would have used an unreachable preferred router, a type B or C host SHOULD send that router a Neighbor Solicitation probe. Probes MUST be limited to no more than one per minute per router. The host need not probe when there is no traffic that would use the router if it were reachable.
sections.plainLanguage: A type C host chooses the most specific matching prefix, then uses preference to break ties. It can periodically check an unreachable preferred router when it has traffic that would use that router.

sections.title: Router Configuration and Examples
sections.content:
Routers SHOULD NOT advertise preferences or routes by default, and SHOULD NOT send their entire routing tables to hosts. They SHOULD advertise no more than 17 Route Information Options per link. Administrators SHOULD configure preferences rather than derive them from routing metrics, and unstable routes SHOULD NOT be advertised until they become more stable.

The RFC recommends that a router without Internet connectivity, or one behind a firewall that blocks general traffic, advertise Low default preference. It also describes a host connected both to a home Internet router and a corporate tunnel: the corporate router can advertise a specific corporate prefix and a Low default preference, sending corporate traffic through the tunnel while general Internet traffic uses the home ISP.
sections.plainLanguage: Administrators should advertise only a small set of stable routes and explicitly configure their preferences. A specific route can direct private-network traffic through a tunnel while other traffic uses another router.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious node could send Router Advertisements with a High preference or specific routes to divert traffic. The RFC notes that similar traffic diversion was already possible by other means and concludes that the extension has no significant incremental impact on Internet infrastructure security.

A malicious node could also advertise an infinite route lifetime or send many route options and frequent advertisements. The RFC says an infinite route lifetime can cause reachability probing to continue indefinitely, but does not itself cause loss of connectivity. It points to RFC 3756 for Neighbor Discovery trust models and threats.
sections.plainLanguage: False Router Advertisements can influence a host's route choice. The RFC says this does not add significant security impact beyond existing Neighbor Discovery risks.
